CleanShot · Operator guide

The Enhance Tab

Everything on the tab, in the order you use it — what each control actually does, how to write a prompt that works, how to read the quality check, and the handful of places the screen will mislead you.

Two things before anything else

Exporting is the only save. There is no Save Project button. An enhanced photo that you never export is gone.

Refreshing the page loses everything. Your prompt, toggles, loaded photos, winner picks and un-exported variants all live in the browser tab. Nothing warns you first. Switching between tabs inside the app is safe; reloading is not.

The short version

  1. Drop in the photos of one machine.
  2. Fill in the equipment details. Make is required now; Model is required later at export, so do both.
  3. Leave both AI models ticked, or untick one.
  4. Write a prompt, or click Insert recommended prompt and edit it.
  5. Flip any add-on toggles you want.
  6. Click Enhance and wait.
  7. For each photo, click the version you want. That’s the winner.
  8. Check the quality flags on anything you’re unsure about.
  9. Export. Nothing is saved until you do.

STEP 1 Load your photos

One drop zone. Drag files in or click it. There is no paste, no camera capture, no URL box, and no way to pull in photos from a previous scan.

  • The limit is 150 photos. Going over is silent — the extras are discarded with no message at all. The N/150 loaded counter is the only thing that tells you.
  • Every file is re-encoded to JPEG and stripped of its EXIF data, whatever its size. Resolution is not reduced — big photos stay big.
  • Drop something that isn’t an image and it’s accepted into the grid, then fails later with a red error on that tile. Nothing stops it at the door.
  • Your filenames are replaced with Make_Model_Year_01.jpg. A preview line under the details card shows exactly what they’ll be called.
  • Remove a single photo with the ✕ on its tile. It only appears on hover, so it’s effectively invisible on a tablet.

Clear all is the destructive one

Clear all empties the grid and throws away the working session behind it. If your batch came in from an import, a reload will not bring it back afterwards. Nothing on screen says so, and there is no undo.

STEP 2 Equipment details

The red card that opens with every batch. Make is the only field the tab requires — but Model is required at export, so filling both now saves you a trip back.

Equipment type is not cosmetic. Ten options in two groups, eight forklift types and two aerial. It changes the anatomy line inside the safety rules — wheel count, fork count, mast stages, counterweight shape — and it hides the fork controls entirely for a scissor lift, which has a platform instead.

Watch the indicator: “✓ Ready to enhance” versus “Enter the Make to continue”.

STEP 3 Choose the models

Two tiles, Gemini and OpenAI, and both start ticked. Each ticked model produces its own version of every photo, so ten photos with both on is twenty generations.

  • You can’t untick both. Clicking the last remaining one does nothing, silently.
  • “Select all” is a trap. It renders already ticked, so your first click on it drops OpenAI and leaves you with Gemini alone. It looks like a “deselect all” and it isn’t.
  • The two aren’t processed identically. Gemini’s output gets an automatic colour lift; OpenAI’s doesn’t. Don’t judge one model’s colour accuracy against the other — you’re not comparing like with like.
  • A blue Retrying pill on an OpenAI variant is normal, not a failure. It gets one automatic re-run if it returns a portrait-shaped image.

The real cost of ticking OpenAI

OpenAI is rate-limited to five images a minute on the server. A 150-photo batch with OpenAI ticked is roughly half an hour of queueing. Nothing on screen says “waiting on a rate limit” — the progress bar simply sits there looking stuck. If you want speed, untick OpenAI.

The ~20s and ~75s badges, and the Fast/Slow labels, are fixed guesses written into the page. They are not measured and they don’t react to how busy the service is.

STEP 4 Write the prompt

This is the part that decides your result, and the part most worth understanding. A prompt is required — without one the Enhance button just tells you to write one.

What you get for free

A block of safety rules is added to every job, after your text, whatever you write. It keeps the real make, model, year and trim; keeps the machine’s anatomy; keeps every OEM make, model, capacity and safety decal exactly where it is, at its original size and wear, still legible; stops lamps, beacons, mirrors, antennas or attachments being added; stops damage being invented; and stops the unit being dropped on a white or studio backdrop, zoomed, cropped, rotated or re-posed.

Don’t spend your prompt restating any of that. It happens anyway.

What you do not get for free

Here is the part that catches everyone. Writing your own prompt replaces the app’s built-in scene description. Five things disappear unless your words carry them:

  1. Tyre treatment — glossy sidewalls but dry, matte tread; and leaving non-marking white or light-grey tyres alone.
  2. Camera angle, lighting direction and background environment.
  3. The honesty line — a cheap shop respray, not a restoration, not factory-fresh.
  4. What the paint doesn’t cover — dents, deep gouges, missing parts and rust-through stay visible.
  5. Paint-job quality — budget finish, slight orange peel, a little overspray.

Decals used to be the one people lost

They aren’t any more — decal preservation is now one of the safety rules, applied on every job whether you mention it or not. You no longer need a “keep every decal” sentence in your prompt.

One thing still needs saying in your own words: a specific instruction about a plate. The rule says “keep every decal as it is”, so it can’t express “change the 50 to an 80” or “the capacity plate is missing, leave it off”. Those are still yours to write.

How long should a prompt be?

Nothing is ever cut off. Your whole prompt reaches the AI that makes the picture, and your whole prompt reaches the checker that reviews it afterwards. Length is a quality question, not a limit.

Shorter still tends to win. The safety rules above are added anyway, so restating them just dilutes what you actually asked for. And the checker treats your prompt as the list of changes to expect — the longer and vaguer that list, the more it lets through. Around 1,500 characters is a good target once the automatic material is stripped out, but it’s a rule of thumb, not a rule.

Two things are never accepted as deliberate no matter how you word it or how long you spend on it: a body panel coming back a different colour family than the original, and non-marking white tyres turned black. Asking for a repaint is not the same as asking to change what colour the machine is.

The Optimize button

Under the prompt box there’s a live character count and a pink Optimize prompt button. It rewrites a long prompt tighter, cutting what the app already adds for you and leaving the five protected items alone.

It shows you Kept and Removed lists and changes nothing until you click again. Read the Kept list. Those are the five above — if one is missing, don’t use the result, because every photo made from it would quietly get worse and still look fine on screen.

There’s also an expandable What gets added to every prompt panel under the box. It lists the safety rules in full, and the five things they don’t cover. Worth reading once.

Prompts worth reusing belong in the shared template library. That has its own short guide: Prompt Templates.

STEP 5 Optional add-ons

Five toggles, all off by default. They append to your prompt rather than replacing it — and because they land after your text, a toggle wins any disagreement with what you wrote.

ToggleWhat it does
Remove Rental-Fleet BrandingStrips third-party rental decals — Sunbelt, United, Herc and the rest. Keeps every OEM decal and the capacity plate.
Perfect Showroom FloorReplaces the floor with clean polished concrete, keeping the unit’s contact shadow. Does nothing on an outdoor photo.
Remove PeopleTakes bystanders out of the frame.
Shine TiresExtra emphasis on tyre dressing for this batch.
Remove Background EntirelyCuts the unit out and exports a transparent PNG. Not a prompt — a separate cut-out step that runs after the image is made.

Remove Background silently cancels Perfect Showroom Floor. There’s no floor left to perfect, but the checkbox stays on and nothing tells you it was ignored.

Toggles reset themselves

Every toggle switches back off automatically when a batch finishes. If you hit ↻ Retry on a variant afterwards, it re-runs with your prompt but without the toggles that produced the original — which is why a retry sometimes comes back noticeably different. Set them again before retrying.

STEP 6 Press Enhance

The button won’t light up until you have a Make and a prompt; until then it displays which one is missing instead of a label.

The percentage on each tile is an animation, not progress. It is not reporting how far along the model is, and it deliberately stops at 95% until the real result lands — so “stuck at 95%” is the normal appearance of waiting, not a symptom.

STEP 7 Read the results

One card per source photo: the original on the left, every model’s version beside it. A ★ Best of N marker means the app’s automatic picker chose that one for you. You can overrule it by clicking any other.

Each variant gives you exactly two tools:

  • ↻ Retry — run it again. Same prompt, but see the toggle warning above.
  • ✎ Tweak — a short typed instruction for a small targeted edit, up to 600 characters. Good for “remove the propane tank”.

There is no erase tool, no crop, no rotate and no brightness control on this tab, whatever older notes may say.

STEP 8 Read the quality check

Every result is checked automatically by three separate AI reviewers that vote independently. This is a safety net against obvious generation failures — a melted mast, a wheel that isn’t there, a model number rewritten into nonsense. It is not a photo critic, and it is told to pass anything good enough to list.

Read the count, not the colour

The pill shows something like 2/3 pass · 84% avg conf. That fraction is the only part you should trust at a glance, for two reasons:

  • PASS and MIXED are drawn in the same colour. A unanimous pass and a split decision look identical. The fraction is what separates them.
  • FAIL is light purple, not red. If you’re scanning for red you will not find it.

The percentage is not a measurement

That confidence figure is the reviewing model’s own opinion of itself, expressed as a number. Nothing measures it and nothing calibrates it. There is no threshold — 62% does not mean “check this one” and 91% does not mean “safe”. Treat it as a tone of voice, not a reading. The verdict and the specific flags are the real output.

The tell: a reviewer that crashed looks like a reviewer that failed you

When one of the three reviewers errors out, it is recorded as a fail with 0% confidence. On the pill that is indistinguishable from a genuine quality problem — your 3/3 quietly becomes 2/3 and you go hunting for a defect that isn’t there.

Expand the per-reviewer breakdown and look at the timing. A real review takes hundreds or thousands of milliseconds. A crashed one reads 0ms. That single number is how you tell “the photo has a problem” from “a checker fell over”.

Reading the individual flags

  • Flags are labelled high, medium or low severity. Medium is drawn in lime — the same green the app uses for “good” everywhere else. It does not mean the flag is fine.
  • Identical-sounding flags from different reviewers get merged. The merge is rough — it groups by defect type plus the first word of the location, so two genuinely different problems in the same general area can collapse into one entry.
  • “No issues found” means the three reviewers didn’t agree on anything specific. It is not a certificate.

If it flags the thing you asked for

The checker reads your whole prompt, so it did see the request — it just wasn’t convinced. Long, vague prompts make this worse, because the instruction gets buried. Tighten it with Optimize prompt so the request is unmissable, and say it plainly.

Two things are never accepted however you phrase them: a panel coming back a different colour family, and white non-marking tyres turned black. Those stay flagged on purpose.

Your own eyes outrank all three reviewers. They exist to catch the embarrassing failure you might miss on a small thumbnail — not to decide whether a photo is good enough to list.

STEP 9 Pick winners

Click the version you want on each card. Clear pick un-chooses it. There is no export button until at least one winner exists, so if Export has vanished, that’s why.

The hold control on a card leaves that image out of the export without un-picking your winner. Useful when one photo of a machine isn’t worth listing but you still want the rest.

STEP 10 Export — the only save

Requires both Make and Model. Every export is 2800 × 2000, a 7×5 shape, set once when the image is enhanced and never resized afterwards.

Images are cover-cropped to that shape, centred — never squashed and never padded. A very tall or very wide source photo will lose its edges. If framing matters, frame it in the camera.

  • The disclaimer watermark is on by default.
  • A transparent-background export comes out as a PNG and carries no watermark.
  • Exported images land in Your Photo Library alongside their originals.
  • Download links expire after an hour. Re-export if one goes stale.

Troubleshooting

What you seeWhat to do
Stuck at 95% for a long timeNormal for a big batch, especially with OpenAI ticked — that’s the five-per-minute limit. Wait.
A tile shows a cut-off red errorPress Retry. The message is truncated and there’s no way to read the rest.
The check says FAIL but the photo looks fineExpand the per-reviewer breakdown. A reviewer reading 0ms crashed — that’s not a verdict on your photo.
It flagged the change I asked forThe request was probably buried in a long prompt. Run Optimize so it reads plainly, then re-enhance.
My retry came back differentToggles reset after a batch. Set them again, then retry.
Forks came back red with yellow tips and I didn’t askThe recommended prompt includes it. Edit that line out.
The Export button isn’t thereNo winner is picked yet. Click a variant.
Yesterday’s work is goneIt wasn’t exported. There is no recovery — export is the only save.

If you only remember two things: export or lose it, and write only what the app doesn’t already do for you — open the “what gets added to every prompt” panel once and you’ll know which half is which.
